items.title: Reid Wiseman, the astronaut shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes
items.summary:
Nasa crew member is fast seeing the similarities between flying Artemis II into lunar orbit and the F1 team’s drive for sporting brilliance

There are characters aplenty within Formula One, a sport that attracts the larger‑than-life, and at the sharp end it can be a parade ground for swaggering egos. Yet the newest addition to the paddock is a man whose quietly spoken, understated thoughtfulness and insight are compelling. Now part of the Mercedes team, Reid Wiseman has been to the moon and with it brings a perspective like no other.

Wiseman was one of four astronauts, alongside Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, who completed the Artemis II lunar flyby in April. Last month Wiseman, the mission’s commander, became an ambassador for Mercedes’ F1 team, formalising a relationship that had been growing over several years, to the delight of his daughter, Katey, a fan of the newly crowned world champion, Kimi Antonelli.

items.t: Reid Wiseman, the astronaut shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes

items.title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports
items.summary:
The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster and the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry

The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

items.title: ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi
items.summary:
Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career

“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

items.title: The Spin | Sandpapergate’s ‘war of the ghosts’ highlights perils of relying on recall
items.summary:
One of Pat Cummins or Usman Khawaja must be lying about Cape Town? Not so, says a professor of memory

In 1932, the English psychologist Frederic Bartlett used cricket as a metaphor for memory. “When I make the stroke I do not, as a matter of fact, produce something absolutely new and I never merely repeat something old” he wrote in his landmark book Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology.

Bartlett posited that remembering the past is just like playing a stroke, a cover drive say, in cricket. You can never repeat the stroke exactly, so like a fingerprint or snowflake, no two cover drives are exactly the same, even when played by the same person. Each cover drive is “manufactured” afresh in the new circumstances, the “schemata of the moment and their interrelations”.

items.title: Child doping isn’t just cheating – it’s a global epidemic of abuse and exploitation | Sean Ingle
items.summary:
Surveys estimate 10 million minors globally use banned performance-enhancing drugs but suppliers are rarely brought to justice

Of all the many stories in Doping Top Secret: Children, a powerful new documentary from the German investigative team that helped expose massive Russian cheating in sport over a decade ago, one keeps replaying in my mind.

It involves an East German champion, who breaks his silence half a century on from his Olympic triumph to reveal how being pumped full of anabolic steroids at a young age accelerated his sexual development and, he believes, dramatically altered his behaviour and those of his teammates. “The system abused me as a young person for the good of the state,” says Hans-Georg Aschenbach, who won ski-jump gold in Innsbruck in 1976. Although nothing can prepare you for what he says about how the drugs affected his libido, and particularly what he would sometimes do before he jumped off a large ramp.

The gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. The role of full-back has changed massively in recent years. We analyse how all 20 sides are approaching the position

Overlapping. Underlapping. Inverted. Traditional. The role of full-back has evolved dramatically. Once a defensive-first position that provided some auxiliary attacking support, the role has developed into something far more multifaceted.

Just ask right-back Ben White, who – with Riccardo Calafiori on the left – has been an important figure in Arsenal’s superb start to the campaign. Talking a few years ago, he said: “Playing full-back the way [Mikel Arteta] wants is completely different to any other manager. To play full-back for him, you’ve got to be a centre-midfielder, a centre-back, a winger and a No 10.”

Springboks’ achievements are remarkable but their head coach lacks statesmanship, diplomacy and good grace in defeat

So here we go again. Exactly five years have passed since South Africa’s head coach, Rassie Erasmus, first felt the full force of World Rugby’s ire for criticising match officials. And guess what? This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly so – for his latest intemperate comments, notable as ever for their total lack of statesmanship, diplomacy or good grace in defeat.

To his acolytes his outspoken nature is part of what makes Rassie such a groot leier (great leader). To many others it simply cements his status as a serial prat. For the avoidance of any doubt everyone respects the remarkable achievements both of Erasmus and his double World Cup-winning teams. It is the rest of the package, sadly, that is too often a major letdown.

items.title: ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future
items.summary:
At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’

After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.

items.title: Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’
items.summary:
In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations

I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group.

As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it.

items.title: I built a reputation as a ‘walker’ so I could cheat when it mattered most – and it worked | The Secret Cricket Coach
items.summary:
Cricket always celebrates sportsmanship and condemns cheating, but where exactly is the line between the two?

I once played in a one-day semi-final. We were in a very tight spot when I edged the ball to the keeper. I didn’t walk. The opposition couldn’t believe it. They crowded around me, furious, and I was getting plenty of abuse.

I managed to get a single and when I reached the other end the umpire said: “You didn’t nick that did you? You are a walker.” “Yep, that’s right,” I replied.
